column5:
I wanted to share some thoughts that might help strengthen our club community and enhance the experience for members across all ages.

At the moment, it can sometimes feel as though our juniors (both primary and intermediate/college age) and adults operate a little separately. It would be great to explore ways to build stronger connections between these groups so the club feels more unified and inclusive for everyone.

Communication is another area where a bit more consistency could make a big difference. At times information is shared across multiple channels, duplicated, or not always easy to find. A clear communication policy—shared with members—could help ensure everyone knows where to look and feels confident they’re receiving the right information at the right time.

It would also be wonderful to celebrate our members’ achievements more visibly. This includes juniors who reach representative level (e.g., NZ Schools) and members who win regional or national titles across any discipline. A consistent approach to acknowledging success would help build pride and connection within the club.

The website could benefit from a refresh, both in terms of design and content. Some information is out of date, and key details can be hard to locate. A more modern layout with essential information prioritised would make it easier for prospective and current members to learn about the club.

Membership information is another area where clearer guidelines could help. Transparency around who pays, who receives discounts, what those discounts cover, and how these decisions are applied would support fairness and confidence across the club.

It may also be helpful to discuss a consistent approach to photography at events—particularly podiums and winners. Many clubs showcase these moments, and having a similar process could help highlight our members’ achievements and promote the club.

Regarding social media, the purpose of the public and private Facebook pages isn’t always clear. The private page appears to include non‑members, which may affect what can be shared—especially personal details like addresses for pack runs. Clarifying the role of each page and ensuring membership is accurately reflected could help with both communication and privacy. The website advertises Facebook, Twitter, Instagram and Strava, are these all actively updated/used/known by members. It would be beneficial for members to understand what each is used for. If they aren't used remove them from the website to avoid confusion. 

We also have people who attend once or twice—whether on Saturdays or Tuesdays—but don’t return. It might be worth considering whether we follow up with these runners, and whether we can learn from the newer “free” running groups that seem to attract and retain people well. Some of these groups also partner with companies to offer discounts, which could be an opportunity for us to explore.

There may also be value in running a charity initiative—such as a “bring a can” event—and inviting local media to cover it. This could help raise the club’s profile and strengthen community engagement.

On that note, it could be helpful to consider how we advertise the club more broadly. There are no formal running clubs in local areas like Tawa, Khandallah, Crofton Downs, or Ngaio. Understanding where runners in these suburbs currently go—and why—might highlight opportunities for growth.

Saturday afternoon pack runs are not heavily attended relative to membership numbers. Some members already run on Sunday mornings, so offering both Saturday afternoon and Sunday morning options could give people more flexibility and potentially increase participation.

Finally, some clubs provide pacers at Parkrun as a way to increase visibility and attract new members. This could be something for us to consider as well.

It would be helpful to understand why the adult and masters track & field awards appear to have been discontinued over the past two years. We still have members who participate in track & field, and some membership categories include this as part of their fee structure. Clarifying whether the awards are paused, being reviewed, or simply need volunteers to support them would help ensure these athletes feel recognized and included and also potentially increase participation.

The club previously offered some excellent guest‑speaker sessions, such as hearing from a nutritionist  and from a club member who had represented New Zealand. These were really valuable and seemed to be well received. They appear to have fallen away in recent years, but it could be worth considering bringing back a small number each year — perhaps two — and planning them in advance.

Topics could include practical areas such as 

Running technique and form — Improving efficiency, reducing injury risk.

Strength training for runners — What to do, how often, and why it matters.

Nutrition for endurance — Fueling before, during, and after training or races.

Mental skills for racing — Confidence, race‑day nerves, pacing mindset.

Goal setting and training planning — How to structure a season or build toward an event.

Masters‑specific training advice — Adjusting training as you age.

Junior development pathways — What helps young runners progress safely.

Trail running skills — Downhill technique, safety, gear.

Race strategy workshops — Pacing, warm‑ups, and how to approach different distances.

Sports psychology — Motivation, resilience, dealing with setbacks.

Community engagement ideas — Charity events, partnerships, visibility.

Basic biomechanics — Understanding how the body moves and how to avoid overload.

There are club members who have the knowledge and experience to be able to deliver some of these sessions. Alternatively would the club consider paying for specialists in these areas to deliver sessions. These types of sessions help build knowledge, confidence, and connection within the club. You could consider opening these sessions up to other clubs and charge a fee to increase revenue.

These ideas are shared with the intention of supporting the club’s ongoing development and helping ensure we continue to be welcoming, connected, and visible in the wider running community.

I’ve already covered many of these points in earlier questions, but I do have a few additional comments.

Regarding the calendar, it would be helpful to clarify whether the question refers to content, format, or where the calendar is located. At the moment, there appears to be some duplication, as the calendar/syllabus is produced both as a PDF and as a month‑view and list‑view on the website. Streamlining this might reduce unnecessary work and make it easier for members to find the information they need.

It would also be useful to know whether the website provides any analytics, such as how many people visit the site, which pages are viewed most often, and which pages receive very little traffic. This type of insight is already available for Facebook, so comparing the two could help the club understand where members prefer to access information.

The newsletter's new format looks great.

The club may also wish to review its communication policy to ensure members know exactly where updates and last‑minute changes will be posted. The recent postponement of the Grand Memorial, which was advised only on Facebook, showed that not all members are aware of where to check for changes. A clear, consistent process for communicating cancellations or updates would help ensure everyone receives information in a timely way.

Having a communication policy will aid in improving website, newsletter, Facebook, and calendar as at present the people who design/deliver/update these work in isolation to each other which leads to duplication, missing or contradictory information.

The club website also lists Twitter, Instagram and Strava, although these aren’t shown as communication channels. Strava, in particular, has been actively used by club members recently, so it may be worth considering whether these platforms should be included or whether members find them useful.

My preferred channel is the newsletter and Facebook.
